## DISCUSSION

We synthesized an FKBP12 presenter-biased DEL to explore the potential of ternary complex DEL

screening aimed at the discovery of FKBP molecular glues. Using protein domains characterized by X-ray

crystallography (structures deposited in the Protein Data Bank), our CIP-DEL screens revealed that

FKBP12 molecular glues can be identified. Interactions with targets were assessed using quantitative

binding measurements of the CIP to the target protein in the absence or presence of FKBP12. We

discovered FKBP12 molecular glues for the bromodomain-containing protein 9 (BRD9) and the non-

bromodomain containing quinoid dihydropteridine reductase (QDPR). These CIPs reconstitute FKBP12

ternary complex formation in both biophysical and cellular assays.

The high-resolution X-ray structures demonstrate that for BRD9, Compound 1 binds the acyl-lysine

binding pocket of BRD9. For QDPR, Compound 4 interacts with a portion of the NADH-binding pocket. In


<!-- Page 11 -->

both cases, only a single hydrogen bond is observed between the molecular glue and the target protein

and the additional remaining compound interactions with the targets are nonpolar interactions, which is a

characteristic of molecular glues and consistent with our inability to demonstrate any significant compound

affinity to the targets alone. Lastly, FKBP12 loops (40s, 50s, 80s) known to contact other molecular glue

targets14 form contacts with both BRD9 and QDPR, while FKBP12 His87 is the only shared protein–protein

contact residue between the two ternary complexes, demonstrating the plasticity of FKBP12 and its ability

to form unique contacts to drive cooperative interactions between disparate targets. Intriguingly, His87 of

FKBP12 also forms protein–protein interactions with mTOR, calcineurin, and CEP250 providing increased

evidence for the importance of the 80’s loop in diverse target recognition14.

Notably, in both FKBP12 ternary complexes, the molecular glues make contacts within hot spots

that mimic interactions with both target’s known endogenous ligands. In the case of BRD9, the Asn216 Nδ2

hydrogen forms an H-bond with a histone’s acyl-lysine carbonyl oxygen and the same Asn216 Nδ2

hydrogen forms an H-bond with Compound 1’s carbonyl oxygen. In addition, the adjacent atoms of

Compound 1 overlay with those of butyryl-lysine, a remarkable ability of a DEL screen to identify moieties

that mimic endogenous ligand interactions without structure-guided design. The CIPs have co-opted

BRD9’s propensity to recognize the PTM, butyryl-Lys, by displaying Compound 1 on the surface of FKBP12,

much like IMiD drugs co-opt cereblon by resembling cereblon’s endogenous C-terminal cyclic imide

degron32.

QDPR is an enzyme that catalyzes the reduction of quinoid dihydrobiopterin into tetrahydrobiopterin

using the cofactor nicotinamide adenine dinucoletide (NADH), which consists of two nucleotides joined

through phosphate groups with each nucleotide containing an adenine base or nicotinamide. This non-

canonical reduction using NADH rather than NADPH distinguishes QDPR from other NAD(P)H-dependent

enzymes33. QDPR Asp41 makes two hydrogen bonds with the cis-hydroxyls on the adenosine ribose ring

of NADH, a highly conserved interaction known to confer selectivity of oxido-reductases for NADH over

NADPH, as NADPH bears a 2’ phosphorylated adenosine ribose34. Compound 4 presents a structural motif

that occupies the region of the QDPR NADH-binding site that overlays only with the adenosine portion of

NADH. Like that observed for NADH, QDPR Asp41 makes one hydrogen bond with the triazine ring of

Compound 4 that occupies the region bound to the adenosine ribose ring of NADH. Similarly to the adenine

ring of NADH, Compound 4 presents a bicyclic ring into the active-site, with key differences, notably a

reversal of the 5-6 membered rings and saturation of the six-membered ring. In addition, as we were able

to assign a single diastereomer based on our X-ray data, we assume that the biochemical and biophysical

binding we observed was due solely to that isomer, and thus the apparent ternary Kd/EC50 of 3.0/3.8 µM is

most likely an underestimate of its true potency. The display of an endogenous ligand mimic (a co-factor in

the case of NADH-QDPR) on the surface of FKBP12 results in a molecular glue binding through a

combination of small molecule-protein and protein–protein interactions. The display from FKBP12 of a

compound having an element that resembles the key motif of the target protein’s substrate, while only

partially occupying the binding site, leverages protein plasticity to form ternary complexes. This feature is

reminiscent of neo-protein-protein interactions resulting from oncogenic missense mutations35.

In this study, we identified and validated molecular glues for two protein targets. Key binding

elements of our screening hits suggest where to focus library expansion in the future. For both BRD9 and

QDPR, the molecular glues are compounds that showed high selectivity for the linker. From the screening

hit profiles for both BRD9 and QDPR, in each case, only 1 of the 44 linkers in the FKBP-CIP DEL library

yielded molecular glues with apparent high cooperativity. Given that for BRD9 the 4-aminopiperidine linker

and for QDPR the spiro [5.2] piperidine based-linker were essential for formation of the ternary complex,

libraries elaborated with an even greater array of linkers may be even more effective. Using multiple FKBP-

ligands and/or exit vectors in the construction of future FKBP-CIP-DELs may yield more opportunities for

FKBP12-target molecular-glue interactions. The FKBP-CIP-DEL from a triazine-scaffold resulted in motifs

that may be too branched and polar for optimal molecular-glue interactions.  Lastly, FKBP-CIP-DEL

libraries, with better predicted ADME properties that also that present flatter/less polar chemistry, as seen

in the macrocyles FK506, rapamycin, and WDB002 could also enable targeting of structural motifs that do

not contain canonically ligandable pockets, such as coiled-coils.

Compound 4 was observed to interact only with the adenosine-binding portion of the QDPR active-

site in our X-ray structure. It is possible that Compound 4, or derivatives, can bring about recruitment of

FKBP12 to other NADH-binding proteins, or even simply adenosine-binding pockets such as ATP binding

We hope to catalyze an expansion in FKBP-molecular glue targets. We believe that continued

## METHODS

FKBP-CIP-DEL library synthesis

The synthesis of FKBP12 CIP-DEL has been reported24. Briefly, as shown in Fig. S10, the FKBP binding

motif was adapted from Ligand 1 in Holt et al.23, where the ester was substituted to an amide to tolerate on-

DNA chemistry, and the cyclohexyl ring was modified to accommodate different connectors that link the

FKBP binding ligand to the triazine library. 44 connector-conjugated FKBP12 binding ligands were

# Development of an FKBP12-recruiting Chemical-Induced Proximity DNA-Encoded Library and its application in discovery of an autophagy potentiator

**Authors:** Zher Yin Tan; Joel K. A. Adade; Xiebin Gu; Cody J. S. Hecht; Michael Salcius; Bingqi Tong; Shuang Liu; Seungmin Hwang; Frédéric J. Zécri; Daniel B. Graham; Stuart L. Schreiber; Ramnik J. Xavier

**Affiliations:** 1Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, Cambridge, MA, 02142, USA | 2Department of Chemistry and Chemical Biology, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA, 02138, USA | 3Novartis Institutes for BioMedical Research, Cambridge, MA, 02139, USA | 4Center for Computational and Integrative Biology, Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, 02114, USA | 5Department of Molecular Biology, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA, 02114, USA | 6Arena BioWorks, Cambridge, MA, 02139 USA | 7Lead contact

## Abstract

Chemical inducers of proximity (CIPs) are molecules that recruit one protein to another and introduce new functionalities toward modulating protein states and activities. While CIP-mediated recruitment of E3 ligases is widely exploited for the development of degraders, other therapeutic modalities remain underexplored. We describe a non-degrader CIP-DNA-Encoded Library (CIP-DEL) that recruits FKBP12 to target proteins using non-traditional acyclic structures, with an emphasis on introducing stereochemically-diverse and rigid connectors to attach the combinatorial library. We deployed this strategy to modulate ATG16L1 T300A, which confers genetic susceptibility to Crohn’s disease, and identified a compound that stabilizes the variant protein against Caspase-3 cleavage in a FKBP12-independent manner. We demonstrate in cellular models that this compound potentiates autophagy, reverses the xenophagy defects, and increases cytokine secretion characteristic of ATG16L1 T300A. This study provides a platform to access unexplored chemical space for CIP design to develop therapeutic modalities guided by human genetics.

## Abstract

## Abstract

Tan et al. designed a DNA-encoded library, comprising compact and diverse linkers, that recruits FKBP12 to any protein of interest to enable efficient discovery of non-degrader proximity inducers. The screen uncovered a compound that stabilized and reversed functional defects of the ATG16L1 T300A IBD risk variant in an FKBP12-independent manner.

## Introduction

Chemical inducers of proximity (CIPs) are small molecules that induce protein-protein interactions (PPIs), allowing one protein to exert its function on the other. By recruiting specific proteins to a target of interest, CIPs provide a versatile platform to develop compounds that can access diverse therapeutic modalities through unexplored mechanisms of action1,2. Indeed, CIPs have been demonstrated to degrade protein targets through the proteasome3,4 or lysosome5,6, alter post-translational modification states including phosphorylation7,8, stabilize certain conformations9, or translocate proteins10,11.

CIPs are typically classified as molecular glues or bifunctional compounds. While many in the field distinguish CIPs based on their chemical structures – bifunctional compounds have a linker joining two separate ligands and molecular glues lack such a linker – we maintain the view that these are distinguished by the cooperativity in ternary complex formation12. Whereas bifunctional compounds bind their target proteins independently with no cooperativity, molecular glues exhibit high cooperativity, with the first binding event promoting the second through formation of a new binding interface or permissive conformational change1,13.

Despite the therapeutic potential and promises of CIPs, their development has traditionally been difficult. Molecular glues are difficult to design de novo and have been typically discovered serendipitously upon studying the mechanisms-of-action for compounds, exemplified by FK50614, rapamycin (Rap)15,16 and thalidomide17. Bifunctional compounds represent an attempt to simplify this problem by linking two known ligands to recruit proteins together18, but in practice these require extensive linker optimization to achieve the intended biological effect3,19.

We have previously employed DNA-encoded libraries (DELs) as a powerful platform to discover both molecular glues and bifunctional degraders that recruit VHL–elongin C–elongin B (VCB) E3 ligase complex to bromodomain (BRD) proteins12,20. DELs are large combinatorial libraries in which each chemical compound is encoded by a DNA tag that records its synthetic history21. This DNA barcode allows compounds to be screened in a pooled format, providing an efficient way of discovering binders against various targets.

Here, we adapted the DEL platform by constructing a DEL containing a binding motif towards a protein to be recruited (presenter protein) to discover CIPs that induce interactions between the presenter protein and any target. To investigate the generalizability of this approach to therapeutic modalities beyond protein degradation, we constructed a CIP-DEL with diverse and stereochemically-defined connectors that recruits FKBP12 and its family members, which are highly expressed in cells, to any target of interest. By comparing enrichments in our screens in the presence or absence of the presenter protein – in this case, FKBP12 – we can distinguish between molecular glues and simple bifunctionals. This allows us to identify CIPs that recruit FKBP12 to targets in a mechanistically relevant manner which is informed by human genetics, potentially leading to broad applications in cell biology beyond protein degradation. To demonstrate the utility of the FKBP12 CIP-DEL, we turned to targets informed by genetic studies that are not amenable to degradation. As part of our longstanding interest in autophagy modulators, we screened our CIP-DEL against ATG16L1 T300A, the product of a loss-of-function Crohn’s Disease (CD) risk genetic variant characterized by defective autophagy-mediated bacterial clearance and increased secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokine interleukin-1β (IL-1β)22–24. We discovered a stabilizer of ATG16L1 T300A that protects the protein from increased susceptibility to Caspase-3 cleavage and reverses the characteristic phenotypic defects. Surprisingly, this compound acts independent of FKBP12, even though the FKBP binding motif is required for activity. Although the compound did not act through the intended mechanism, this study highlights the possibility of discovering compounds with interesting biological function, while serving a cautionary tale on unexpected modes of actions arising from rationally designed screens.

## Design

### Design and synthesis of an FKBP12 CIP-DEL

Our group and others previously employed CIP-DELs for the discovery of degraders by recruiting E3 ligases12,25. To expand the applications of CIP-DEL to non-degrader modalities, we chose FKBP12 as the presenter protein for our initial study for the following reasons. It is highly expressed in various cell types, allowing any CIP to recruit it efficiently. While FKBPs are prolyl-isomerase, we hypothesized that their recruitment could serve as a steric block to disrupt PPIs, or bind to traditionally hard-to-drug targets by engaging the large protein surface for hydrophobic interactions. Recruitment of FKBP12 to targets has been demonstrated by both natural14,15,26 and synthetic compounds27,28, and the availability of drugs (such as tacrolimus and sirolimus) working through this mechanism implies that there would not be negative effects by binding FKBP12. Furthermore, analysis of the CIP-mediated ternary complexes formed by FKBP12 and various targets show differences in the FKBP12 binding surface26, providing a high degree of flexibility and improving the odds of binding with additional targets. While many examples of macrocyclic FKBP12-recruiting molecular glues have been reported14,15,26,28, acyclic FKBP12 glues have not been widely explored27, even though acyclic binders have seen widespread use as bifunctional tool compounds11,29,30. Other FKBP members share a highly conserved binding site with FKBP1231, and are demonstrated to bind to FKBP12 ligands32, which implies that any FKBP12-recruiting library could recruit the other FKBPs as well.

We designed the non-degrader FKBP12 CIP-DEL (Fig. 1A) based on a small but potent FKBP12 binder 1 (Ki = 7 nM) with an X-ray crystal structure (PDB: 1FKH)33. The pipecolic acid core with the ketoamide-group mimics proline, the natural substrate of FKBP12, and is the key to maintaining interaction with FKBP12. The para-position of the phenyl ring on the binder points towards solvent, and the corresponding position on FK506 and Rap has been functionalized with linkers for attaching to beads for pull down studies34. For these reasons, we targeted this phenyl ring as an ideal vector for placement of the DNA tag while maintaining binding towards FKBP12. Upon examining the crystal structures of FKBP12-bound compound 1 and other FKBP12-recruiting compounds, the cyclohexyl group points towards the interface of the protein-protein interactions, and we surmised this will be an appropriate exit vector to attach a combinatorial library to interact with target proteins. While the positions of the DNA tag and combinatorial library could be swapped, we opted for a design closer to FK50635,36 and Rap37 to increase our odds of success. We synthesized a few analogs based on this design, swapping the ester for an amide to better tolerate subsequent on-DNA chemistry, specifically the Nosyl-deprotection and the 3rd SNAr steps, and confirmed that FKBP12 binding is retained via a Time-Resolved-Förster’s Resonance Energy Transfer TR-FRET based binding assay, albeit diminished from the parent molecule 1, with micromolar potency (Fig. S1A). While the initial design is based on ligand binding to FKBP12, all FKBP members share a conserved binding site31, and therefore it is likely that this library could recruit the other FKBP family members in physiological settings.

## Results

Our previous work revealed the significance of connectors in participating in the BRD4-CIP-VHL ternary complex formation, with the connectors forming contacts with both proteins, contributing to binding rather than acting as a mere linker of two ligands12,20. Taking this into consideration, we designed a diverse set of rigid, compact, stereochemically-defined diamines as connectors, drawing inspiration from diversity-oriented synthesis38,39 and stereochemical probe libraries40,41 (Fig. 1B and Fig. S1B). Several PEG-containing linkers typically used in traditional bifunctional molecules are also included. To characterize the chemical space accessible by the connectors from the FKBP12 binding site, we constructed a model of the connector acetylated at one amine (representing the FKBP12 binding motif) and a free amine at the other end which would be connected to the triazine library. To assess the 3D space covered by the connectors from the FKBP12 binding site, we anchored the acetyl group and projected the conformations of the connectors outwards (Fig. 1C). By observing the position and the directions of the C-N bonds, it is clear that the connectors are able to project the library out uniformly from the FKBP12 binding site at various angles and distances away from the amide bond, fully capturing a wide space from the exit vector. Low energy conformations of the model compounds were plotted in a principal moment of inertia (PMI) plot, which reveal many sphere-like and disc-like conformations in addition to the expected rod-like conformations (Fig. S1C).

DEL precursor 3 was chosen as the starting point for the FKBP CIP-DEL. The solvent-facing phenyl ring was substituted with a para-phenol group to provide a synthetic handle, which was propargylated and linked to azido-DNA-headpiece via copper(I) catalyzed azide-alkyne click (CuAAC) reaction. Lastly, the cyclohexyl group was replaced with a carboxylic acid for attachment to diamine connectors (Cycle 1), which can be subsequently linked to a triazine library for adding two amine building blocks (Cycles 2 and 3) via sequential nucleophilic substitutions (SNAr).

The connectors were converted into mono-N-protected diamines for DNA-compatible deprotection from the mono-tert-butyloxycarbonyl (mono-Boc) protected diamines, via a series of protecting group manipulations to achieve protection on either amine. We chose the classic triazine library to exploit the large diversity of accessible amines, with the added advantage of cross-library comparisons with our previously described DELs12,20. The final amine building blocks included in the library are identical to those used in the VHL-recruiting library that we previously developed20.

The initial plan of adding connectors on-DNA proved to be challenging. While attaching carboxylic acids to amine on-DNA is routinely performed, we did not achieve sufficient efficiency with the reverse amidation (where amines are added to acids on-DNA). Furthermore, upon activation of the acid, the neighboring amide can perform a nucleophilic addition-elimination to produce a stable five-membered ring (Fig. S1D). To circumvent this, the amidation to install connectors was performed off-DNA, followed by in situ CuAAC onto the azide-modified DNA headpiece (Fig. 1D). The DNA-conjugates with 44 different connectors were then separately purified by preparative UPLC, which enabled pure products from Cycle 1 to be incorporated into the library. After encoding the Cycle 1 DNA-conjugates by ligation of DNA tags, we added on the triazine scaffold via SNAr, and performed two rounds of split-pool synthesis to install the 290 amines in the 2nd SNAr and 249 amines in the 3rd SNAr to result in a 3.2 million-membered-FKBP12 CIP-DEL. This CIP-DEL occupies a distinct chemical space from known FKBP12-recruiting CIPs26–28,42 (Fig. 1E), allowing us to access unexplored chemical space and complement existing binders.

## Results

### Screen for autophagy inducers

To demonstrate the utility of the approach, we set out to screen for a compound that recruits FKBP12 to an ‘undruggable’ target with human disease relevance, focusing on genetic variants impacting broadly important cell biological processes. We have a longstanding interest in discovering small molecules that modulate autophagy43–45. Macroautophagy (or autophagy) is an important cellular homeostatic and survival process whereby unwanted cytoplasmic contents, organelles or pathogens are targeted for lysosomal degradation46. GWAS studies have uncovered genetic variants in the ATG genes that increase susceptibility towards various diseases46. In particular, the T300A coding variant of ATG16L1 has been associated with increased risk of Crohn’s disease (CD)22. ATG16L1 is an adaptor that is important for maturation of the autophagosome and is indispensable for autophagy. Biochemical studies have revealed that the protein harboring this loss-of-function mutation is more susceptible to cleavage by Caspase-3 (Casp3), which decreases the intracellular stability of ATG16L1 and leads to impaired autophagy23,24. We hypothesized that FKBP12, when recruited close to the ATG16L1 T300A protein, could act as a shield to hinder Casp3 from approaching, thereby indirectly stabilizing ATG16L1 and potentially restoring autophagic flux and mitigating downstream phenotypes (Fig. 2A). Increasing the activity of ATG16L1 could dampen pro-inflammatory cytokine responses47, as well as strengthen host-mediated clearance of intracellular pathogens (also known as xenophagy)48 in the intestines, providing an innovative approach for broad anti-infective therapeutics.

### Discovery of FKBP-DEL hits against ATG16L1 T300A

To screen the FKBP12 CIP-DEL against ATG16L1 T300A protein, we designed constructs truncated at the N-terminus of ATG16L1, which interacts with other ATG proteins and is important for function. We expressed and purified ATG16L1 T300A truncated to either E44 or M117 on the N termini, both of which lack the helix that interacts with ATG5-12. We selected the M117 truncation construct for screening, as the E44 construct could not be immobilized onto our DEL screening beads; we retained the longer E44 truncation construct for subsequent validation experiments. The screening workflow to discover binders or CIPs to ATG16L1 is similar to approaches taken in our previous work12,20, and is illustrated in Figure 2b. Briefly, we immobilized His-tagged ATG16L1 with Co2+ coated magnetic beads, and co-incubated them with either library [beads, target, library (BTL)], or library with tagless FKBP12 [beads, target, library, presenter (BTLP)] at 2, 6, and 20 μM. We also incubated the library with the beads alone as a control to identify nonspecific binders [beads, library (BL)]. After several washing steps, the binders were released from beads and the DNA barcodes were amplified by PCR and purified by gel extraction. To call hits from the screen, we modeled sequencing counts as a Poisson distribution and compared the lower bound of the 95% confidence interval of the ratios between conditions for a more conservative scoring to reduce false positives49. The target protein ATG16L1 T300A is in large excess compared to each individual library member, which reduces the competition of open binding sites on the target. We define binary enrichment as BTL/BL, ternary enrichment as BTLP/BL, and the presenter ratio as BTLP/BTL; previous work shows that enrichment is correlated with binding strength, while the presenter ratio is correlated to cooperativity12 (Fig. 2C). Bead binders will show low enrichment ratios and will be filtered out. Importantly, we predict that binders or bifunctionals will show high binary and ternary enrichments with low presenter ratios, while glues will show high ternary enrichment and high presenter ratio.

Some compounds exhibited high ternary enrichment in 3D graphs of the screen hits, with most of the top hits containing the aminothiazole building block 220 in cycle 3 (Fig 2D). When ternary enrichment was plotted against the presenter ratio, we observed that the highly enriched compounds had low presenter ratios, indicating that FKBP12 does not improve binding of hits towards ATG16L1 (Fig. S2A). Some compounds that show high presenter ratios but the counts were too low to be reliable. This enrichment trend is identical for screens with varying concentrations of soluble FKBP12 (Fig. S2B), suggesting that the hits act more as binders or bifunctional compounds instead of cooperative glues, and might tolerate simultaneous binding to both FKBP12 and ATG16L1. The prevalence of building block 220 across hits also suggests its importance in binding, and this provides more confidence in the hits. The lack of selectivity of the cycle 1 building blocks suggests that the connector is not as crucial, which further supports the hits being bifunctional molecules instead of glues. However, it is interesting to note that the PEG-containing linkers did not show up in the highly enriched hits. We performed a DEL-screen using a 7 million-membered triazine library as well, and the enriched hits contain the same building block in cycle 3 (Fig. S2C), further increasing our confidence in the hits. Considering that ATG16L1 has no known small molecule binders, the possibility of having binders or bifunctional compounds could serve as tool compounds for studying ATG16L1 biology. Taking both the raw counts and enrichment ratios from all screening conditions (ATG16L1 T300A with 0, 2μM, 6μM, 20μM additional FKBP12) into account, we selected and synthesized six compounds off-DNA with at least two shared building blocks between them for further validation (Fig. 2E and Table S1). We also referenced the top hits from the triazine screen for hit selection, and A3B was chosen as it shares a building block with very similar structure to the top triazine hits (Fig. S2D). The synthesized compounds were confirmed to bind to FKBP12 in the TR-FRET assay (Fig. 2E), although the potencies were reduced compared to the analogs in the preliminary study (Fig. S1A).

### A3B reduces Casp3 mediated cleavage of ATG16L1 T300A

To determine the activity of compounds on ATG16L1 cleavage, we developed an AlphaLISA-based biochemical assay to measure levels of intact ATG16L1 (Fig. 3A). We recombinantly expressed ATG16L1 T300A protein truncated at E44 with an N-terminal His tag and a C-terminal Flag tag, which can associate with nickel Alpha donor beads and anti-flag AlphaLISA acceptor beads, respectively. The protein was added to a 384 well plate containing DMSO control or 20 μM of compound and incubated for one hour. Recombinant Casp3 was then added to cleave ATG16L1 T300A, and after one hour the reaction was quenched by addition of Caspase-3 inhibitor z-DEVD-FMK (CaspIn). Intact ATG16L1 exhibits high AlphaLISA signal as the two beads will be in close proximity, whereas signal will be diminished once ATG16L1 is cleaved. Of the six synthesized compounds subjected to the AlphaLISA assay, A3B appeared as the sole hit (Fig. 3B). The levels of intact and cleaved ATG16L1 T300A after the reaction were also visualized by western blot (Fig. 3C), which provided results consistent with the AlphaLISA assay. A3B had an EC50 of 12.1 μM, and similar results were observed in the presence or absence of FKBP12 (Fig. 3D) in ATG16L1 T300A. A similar EC50 of 11.5 μM was obtained for the WT ATG16L1 (Fig. S3A). We synthesized the control compounds of A3B (Fig. 3E) without the FKBP12 binding motif (A3Bt), the triazine library (F31) or the common building block (A3Bp) and found that those compounds were inactive or had attenuated activity (Fig. 3F). To ensure that the compounds were not inhibiting Casp3, a counter screen with a fluorescent Casp3 substrate was performed and none of the compounds inhibited Casp3 activity directly (Fig. S3B). Unexpectedly, the addition of FKBP12 did not alter the activity of A3B, showing that A3B stabilizes ATG16L1 in an FKBP12-independent manner, acting as a monovalent compound instead of a CIP. As A3B only weakly binds to FKBP12 (EC50 = 30μM), it could bind FKBP12 at the higher concentrations in the dose-curve, but is unlikely to fully compete against ATG16L1 binding. In this case, FKBP12 recruitment is not needed for activity. However, the observation that the full A3B molecule is needed for the effect was unexpected and implies a contribution of the FKBP12 binding motif towards ATG16L1 protection from Casp3 cleavage. This is further supported by the ester containing analog A3Be, where the substitution of amide to ester led to a loss in activity in the ATG16L1 cleavage assay, suggesting that the amide on the FKBP binding motif forms key interactions with ATG16L1 (Fig. S3C). This unexpected finding exemplifies the challenges in identifying CIPs even with a biasing element, but highlights the utility of accessing diverse chemical space via CIP-DEL libraries.

### A3B potentiates autophagy in cells

To investigate the biological functions of the compounds, we measured autophagy using a GFP-LC3 reporter HeLa cell line50. LC3 is a ubiquitin-like protein that is conjugated to the autophagosome membrane via the E3-like conjugation system, in which ATG16L1 plays an essential role. Thus, the function of ATG16L1 in the autophagy pathway can be monitored through GFP-LC3 puncta formation, a whole marker of the autophagosome before its degradation through lysosomal fusion. Given the hypothesis that A3B stabilizes ATG16L1, we predicted that cells treated with A3B alone would have low levels of LC3 puncta formation, while co-treatment with inducers of autophagy would lead to a synergistic increase in LC3 puncta levels. Indeed, this was observed in our results, where co-treatment with 5μM Rap or 2μM Torin1, mTOR inhibitors that induce autophagy51, lead to drastic synergistic increases in LC3 puncta area compared to A3B treatment alone (Fig. 4A). While both Rap and Torin1 inhibit mTOR, Rap requires FKBP12 recruitment for its activity37. The observation that A3B is active with co-treatment of both of these compounds further supports the notion that A3B acts independently of FKBP12. This phenotype in the puncta assay is recapitulated by co-treatment of Caspase-3 inhibitor with DMSO, Rap or Torin1 (Fig. S4A), which is consistent with the hypothesis that A3B stabilizes ATG16L1 against Casp3 inhibition. It is notable that other DEL hits (A1A, A1B, A3A) are active in the LC3 puncta formation assay, but were not active in the Casp3 cleavage assay, suggesting that there might be additional mechanisms causing this phenotype which warrants further investigations. A3B alone induced GFP-LC3 puncta formation to a small extent with an EC50 of 12.0 μM, while the magnitude of puncta formation is further increased in the presence of Rap (EC50 = 11.5 μM) or Torin1, which did not see saturation even at 80 μM (Fig. 4B). The magnitude of increase in LC3 puncta appears to be correlated with the magnitude of autophagy induction, suggesting that A3B acts as a potentiator of autophagy. Upon siRNA-mediated depletion of ATG16L1, the level of LC3 puncta formation is reduced for all conditions, as ATG16L1 is essential for autophagy. There is still an increase in LC3 puncta upon treatment with Rap or Torin1, but the A3B-mediated increase was strongly diminished (Fig. 4C), showing that ATG16L1 is required for A3B’s activity for inducing autophagy. The control compounds A3Bt and F31, either alone or in combination (A3Bt + F31) did not show an increase in LC3 puncta formation (Fig. 4D), suggesting that the full molecule is required for binding towards ATG16L1 and is necessary for LC3 induction. A3Bp shows a much more attenuated increase in GFP-LC3 puncta formation in the presence of Rap (Fig. 4D), which highlights the importance of building block 220 (Fig. 2D) and is consistent with the screening results.

In response to autophagy induction, LC3-I (unlipidated LC3) is converted to LC3-II (lipidated) and accumulates on the autophagosome; the ratio of LC3-II to LC3-I is correlated to autophagic flux. To complement our LC3 puncta assay, we assessed the accumulation of LC3-II in ATG16L1 KO HeLa cells reconstituted with either wild type (WT) or T300A ATG16L1. Addition of 20 μM A3B increased the LC3-II to LC3-I ratio compared to DMSO control, and co-treatment with Rap also resulted in an increased LC3-II to LC3-I ratio compared to Rap alone in both WT and ATG16L1 T300A HeLa cells (Fig. 4E). The LC3-II to LC3-I ratio can increase upon induction of autophagy but also upon blocking of autophagosome degradation through lysosomal fusion. When co-treated with 100nM BafA1, a lysosomal inhibitor, A3B increased LC3-II to LC3-I compared to BafA1 treatment alone (Fig. 4E), suggesting that A3B acts by increasing autophagic flux rather than inhibiting autophagosome degradation50. This phenotype was also recapitulated by monitoring endogenous LC3 puncta via immunofluorescence, further supporting the notion that A3B increases autophagic flux (Fig. S4B).

To further validate the biological activity of A3B, we turned to bone marrow derived macrophages (BMDMs) from GFP-LC3 reporter mice harboring the ATG16L1 T300A mutation to measure the impact on autophagy in primary cells. While compounds alone did not increase the number of GFP-LC3 puncta when the cells were in complete media, cells starved in HBSS media (another method of inducing autophagic flux) showed a substantial increase in GFP-LC3 puncta area when treated with A3B but not the control compounds (Fig 4F). A3B induced GFP-LC3 puncta formation in starved GFP-LC3 BMDMs with an EC50 of 22.7 μM at 4 hours (Fig. S4B). This is in close agreement with the results obtained for the GFP-LC3 HeLa cells with wild-type ATG16L1. To further probe whether A3B induces or inhibits autophagy, we co-treated GFP-LC3 BMDMs with A3B and Bafilomycin A1 (BafA1) in complete media or HBSS, and observed an increased LC3-II to LC3-I ratio with A3B + BafA1 compared to BafA1 alone (Fig. S4D). While treating starved GFP-LC3-expressing ATG16L1 T300A BMDMs with A3B and BafA1, we observed a further increase in LC3 puncta compared to treatment with BafA1 alone (Fig. S4E). Taken together, these data corroborate that A3B increases or potentiates autophagic flux through stabilization of ATG16L1.

### A3B reverses deleterious effects of T300A mutation in bacterial clearance and IL-1β secretion

After confirming that A3B increases autophagic flux synergistically in the presence of an additional autophagy stimulus, we investigated the functional effects of A3B in biological processes disrupted by ATG16L1 loss-of-function. To probe the effect of A3B on xenophagy, we first infected ATG16L1 KO HeLa cells reconstituted with either WT or T300A ATG16L1 with S. Typhimurium for 30 mins, followed by treatment with A3B or other control compounds at 20 μM for 6 hours. We found that the T300A variant resulted in a higher S. Typhimurium colony forming units (CFUs) compared to the wild type, which is consistent with prior work23,24 (Fig. 5A). A3B was able to reduce S. Typhimurium CFUs in both WT and T300A cell lines, reversing the defect in bacterial clearance caused by the T300A mutation (Fig. 5A). A3B also reduced the S. Typhimurium CFUs in the ATG16L1 KO HeLa cells, suggesting that A3B is engaging other targets in addition to ATG16L1 that lead to intracellular bacterial clearance. To further assess dependence of A3B-mediated bacterial control on ATG16L1, we tracked the growth of bioluminescent S. Typhimurium-infected WT HeLa, ATG16L1 KO, and ATG16L1 KO reconstituted with ATG16L1 WT (Fig. S5A). Without A3B treatment, ATG16L1 KO increased Salmonella growth drastically, and this increase was reversed by reconstituting ATG16L1. At early time points, A3B did not significantly reduce the S. Typhimurium bioluminescence compared to DMSO control in the ATG16L1 KO cell line, while both the WT and ATG16L1-reconstituted cells exhibited consistently lower levels of S. Typhimurium bioluminescence when treated with A3B. However, after 6 hours of A3B treatment, S. Typhimurium growth was reduced in the ATG16L1 KO cells as well compared to DMSO-treatment, suggesting that A3B engages in other pathways that contribute to intracellular bacterial clearance at later time points. The control compounds had either no activity or attenuated activity in reducing CFU, consistent with the GFP-LC3 puncta assay in HeLa cells (Fig. S5B). The growth curve of S. Typhimurium in the presence of 20 μM A3B was similar to that of DMSO control, demonstrating that A3B had no effect on axenic bacterial growth (Fig. S5C). Using the GFP-LC3 HeLa cells, we observed large GFP-positive puncta selectively forming around S. Typhimurium (Fig. 5B), suggesting that increased targeting of the bacteria promotes xenophagy to aid in bacterial clearance.

Finally, we sought to further investigate the biological effects of A3B on cytokine imbalance observed with the ATG16L1 T300A variant. Depletion of ATG16L152 and the T300A mutation23,24, both lead to increased IL-1β secretion upon inflammasome activation, and we sought to investigate whether A3B modulates this phenotype. Upon priming BMDMs with lipopolysaccharide (LPS) followed by the addition of ATP to activate the inflammasome53, we show that ATG16L1 T300A was associated with increased secretion of IL-1β compared to WT cells (Fig. 5C). Treatment with A3B reduced IL-1β secretion in both cell lines, further exemplifying the potential of A3B to reverse the deleterious effects of the T300A variant. We performed CRISPR-Cas9 mediated knockout of ATG16L1 in WT BMDMs, and observed an increase in IL-1β secretion when ATG16L1 is depleted in the DMSO control treatment, consistent with previous reports54. A3B-mediated reduction is diminished in ATG16L1 knockout cells compared to unedited cells, exemplifying the role of ATG16L1 in A3B’s activity (Fig. S5D). However, there was still a significant reduction in IL-1β secretion in the ATG16L1-depleted cells upon A3B treatment, suggesting that A3B engages in other pathways that partially contribute to the phenotype as well. While the A3B-mediated increase in LC3 puncta is decreased upon genetic depletion of ATG16L1, the functional assays in intracellular clearance and IL-1β secretion are not as selective and are partly mediated by ATG16L1-independent effects from A3B. Taken together, we built a library to discover CIPs that recruit FKBP12 to targets, and discovered A3B, an FKBP12-independent stabilizer of ATG16L1, that promotes autophagy in cells.

## Discussion

While we learn more about human health and disease through various genomics studies, it is clear that creative chemistry and unexplored therapeutic hypotheses are required to tackle these targets and challenges. CIPs represent a versatile platform that expands functionalities of small molecules to broaden our therapeutic toolbox. While target protein degradation has dominated the field, there are many other modalities that can be exploited through simple induction of neo-PPIs or recruitment of non-degradative effector proteins. To explore this further, we adapted the DEL platform to recruit other proteins by incorporating a presenter protein binding motif. To this end, we’ve designed and synthesized a 3.2 million membered-CIP-DEL aimed to identify CIPs that recruit FKBP12 to any target of interest. FKBP12 is highly expressed in the cell and can be easily recruited to perform the intended function. Furthermore, the FKBP binding motif in the DEL can recruit other FKBPs32, allowing for compensatory effects if FKBP12 is mutated or depleted. CIPs developed with this motif might be less susceptible to resistance if applied to oncology, which is another advantage of this CIP-DEL.

Genomic studies have uncovered many targets that require development of approaches for therapeutic intervention, and our study focuses on ATG16L1 as one such example. ATG16L1 is a scaffolding protein required for the initiation of autophagy, and the T300A mutation renders this protein more susceptible to Casp3-mediated cleavage. We hypothesized that by recruiting FKBP12 to ATG16L1, it can act as a steric, block to hinder the approach of Casp3 and indirectly stabilize the protein. The hit compound A3B was able to reduce Casp3 mediated cleavage of ATG16L1, and the presence of the FKBP binding motif was important for its activity, even though FKBP12 protein was unexpectedly not required for its in vitro activity. A3B was able to potentiate autophagy using various stimuli, for both WT and T300A ATG16L1 in cell line and primary macrophages, in an ATG16L1-dependent manner. A3B was also able to reverse the deleterious phenotypes of the T300A variant in bacterial clearance and IL-1β secretion, although it still shows activity in the ATG16L1-depleted cells, suggesting A3B could be engaging in other targets to contribute to these functional effects downstream of autophagy. Taken together, A3B was able to enhance the cellular activity of ATG16L1 and reverse the phenotypes of the risk variant, and could serve as a starting point for therapeutic development in the future.

Unlike other CIPs which recruit an effector protein to a target protein, it is crucial to ascertain the role of FKBP12 recruitment towards the activity of these CIPs. In our case, the biochemical assay shows A3B is active regardless of FKBP12, but activity is lost without the FKBP12 binding motif. If we consider the FKBP12 binding motif as being important for ATG16L1 binding, addition of FKBP12 should compete with A3B and result in loss of activity, which was not observed. This can be rationalized by the weaker binding to FKBP12 compared to ATG16L1, and A3B exerts its effect in a monovalent manner independent of FKBP12 recruitment. A3B could bind close to the cleavage site or induce a conformational change which reduces ATG16L1 T300A susceptibility to Casp3 cleavage, and this merits further studies in the future to understand the binding mode of A3B. Similar findings were reported in the literature, whereby some FKBP binding macrocycles bind to their target regardless of the availability of FKBP proteins55,56. Related studies show different behaviors of FKBP-recruiting molecules, where some exhibit increased potency with additional FKBP28,30, and others take advantage of FKBP12 binding to partition into the cell57. A deeper understanding in the differing behavior of such molecules would be important in developing and advancing CIPs that recruit FKBP12 or other presenter proteins.

Our work highlights an approach of designing CIPs to interrogate potential therapeutic modalities depending on the desired mechanisms for specific targets with unique functions. Our library is constructed in a way that allows for easy design of control compounds for SAR studies and experiments to interrogate the role of FKBP12 in an observed phenotype. These will be crucial to further studies to determine the mechanisms of action of hit compounds. Overall, our study presents a non-degrader platform that can be easily adapted to recruit any protein of interest and that expands our repertoire of tools to modulate various biological processes.

### Limitations of the study

The platform we developed here identified a compound that requires the FKBP12 binding motif to mitigate the phenotypic effects of our target variant protein, however, it was unexpected that the function of this compound would be independent of FKBP12. While this study demonstrated a hit with interesting biological activity, more screens and data will be needed to assess the hit rate of the library, in terms of identifying glues, bifunctional compounds and binders. Lastly, there might be promiscuous building blocks in the library against certain target classes that are yet to be identified, but these will be better understood as we deploy the library for additional screens.

## STAR Methods

### EXPERIMENTAL MODEL AND STUDY PARTICIPANT DETAILS

#### Cell Lines

All cells were cultured at 37°C with 5% CO2. HeLa cells (female) were cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) supplemented with 10% Fetal bovine serum (Sigma; F0392), 1X Glutamax (Invitrogen; 35050-061) and 0.375% sodium bicarbonate, unless otherwise noted. ATG16L1 KO Hela cells, as well as ATG16L1 KO cells reconstituted with WT or T300A ATG16L1, were generated by Begun et al.58 Mycoplasma testing is routinely performed on cell lines using Universal Mycoplasma Detection Kit (ATCC; 30-1012K). All BMDMs (derived from male and female mice) were cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) supplemented with 10% Fetal bovine serum (Sigma; F0392), 1X Glutamax (Invitrogen; 35050-061), 1% non-essential amino acid (Life Technologies Corporation; 11140076), 0.375% sodium bicarbonate and 20 ng/mL M-CSF (Peprotech; 315-02).

#### Mice

ATG16L1 T300A C57BL/6 mice were previously generated by Lassen et al.24 Wild type mice used in this study were offspring of heterozygous ATG16L1 T300A C57BL/6 breeding pairs. GFP-LC3 transgenic59 mice were a gift from Noboru Mizushima. T300A mice and GFP-LC3 mice were crossed to generate T300A GFP-LC3 mice. Mice were maintained over several generations at Massachusetts General Hospital. Experiments involving these mice were conducted under protocol 2003N000158 approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) at Massachusetts General Hospital. Mice ranging in age from 3-18 wk old were used in this study across different experiments. For harvesting BMDMs, 8-12 wk old mice were used, without selecting for sex. For experiments comparing ATG16L1 WT and T300A, littermate controls were used.

### METHOD DETAILS

#### Molecular modeling of connectors

Mono-acetylated diamines were generated as model compounds for the connectors. Conformational search was performed using the Conformational Search tool in MOE (Method: LowModeMD), and the resulting conformers were aligned at the acetyl group. The non-acetyl carbon atoms were hidden for clarity.

#### Diversity of library

The libraries were enumerated using RDKit in KNIME (https://www.rdkit.org/). The Morgan fingerprint was generated for each compound, and the RDKit Diversity Picker Node was used to choose the top 1000 most diverse compounds in each library. The resulting fingerprints were used to train a UMAP embedding and plotted in Python.

#### PMI plot

Model compounds of the connectors were linked to acetyl group on one end and dichlorophenyl on the other were generated for the connectors. Conformational search was performed using the Conformational Search tool in MOE (Method: LowModeMD). The Principal Moment of Inertia (PMI)-Derived Properties node and PMI Triangle Scatter Plot Nodes from Vernalis Research were used to generate the PMI plot for the resulting conformers using KNIME.

#### CIP-DEL Affinity screening

The CIP-DEL screening was performed with 5 different selection conditions in parallel: (1) beads-only control (BL: beads, library), (2) ATG16L1 - FKBP12 (BTL: beads, target protein, library), and (3) ATG16L1 T300A M117 (Table S2) + 2/6/20 μM FKBP12 (BTLP: beads, target protein, library, presenter protein). The screening buffers used are ‘B (binding) Buffer’ containing 25 mM HEPES pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, 0.05% Tween-20 (w/v), and ‘S (selection) Buffer’ containing 25 mM HEPES, pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, 0.05% Tween-20 (w/v), and 0.3 mg/mL Ultrapure Salmon Sperm DNA (ThermoFisher Scientific 15632011).

Dynabeads His-Tag Isolation and Pulldown beads (Invitrogen 10103D, 10 μL per sample) were manually washed three times with B buffer and resuspended in B buffer (100 μL per sample). Using a KingFisher Duo Prime (Thermo Scientific 5400110) in a 96-well deepwell plate (Thermo Scientific 95040452) at rt, the washed beads were transferred to His-tagged ATG16L1 (2 μM in B buffer, 100 μL per sample) for ATG16L1 immobilization (30 mins, medium mix). The beads were washed once with B buffer (200 μL) and twice with S buffer (200 μL) (3 min each, medium mix). The beads were then incubated (1 h, medium mix) with the library (10 million copies per library member, 100 μL in S buffer) only, or the library preincubated with tagless FKBP12 (2 μM in S buffer). The beads were then washed once with S buffer (200 μL) and twice with B buffer (200 μL) (3 min each, medium mix). Finally, the beads were transferred to B buffer (100 μL) and heated (95 °C, 5 min) to elute bound DEL members into the supernatant.

The supernatant was removed and the eluted barcodes were quantified by qPCR. Successful immobilization of the ATG16L1 protein was checked by resuspending the beads in NuPAGE LDS Sample Buffer (133.3 μL of 1×) supplemented with TCEP (3.33 μL of 0.5 M), heating at 95 °C for 5 min, and loading the supernatant onto an SDS-PAGE gel. The barcodes of the eluted DEL were PCR amplified using i5 and i7 index primers using Platinum Hot Start PCR Master Mix (Invitrogen). The PCR products were cleaned up using the ChargeSwitch PCR Clean-Up Kit, pooled in equimolar amounts, and the 187 bp amplicon was gel purified using 2% E-Gel EX Agarose Gels (ThermoFisher Scientific G401002) and the QIAquick Gel Extraction Kit (Qiagen 28704). The DNA concentration was measured using the Qubit dsDNA BR assay kit and sequenced using a HiSeq SBS v4 50 cycle kit (Illumina FC-401-4002) and HiSeq SR Cluster Kit v4 (Illumina GD-401-4001) on a HiSeq 2500 instrument (Illumina). The sequencing data were analyzed as previously described49 and reported as the lower bound of 95% confidence interval, unless stated otherwise. A step-by-step protocol can be found in Protocol S1.

#### FKBP12 binding assay

FKBP12 binding was determined using an N-terminal biotinylated FKBP12 protein and a FITC-labeled SLF compound in TR-FRET. Compounds were dispensed using an Echo acoustic dispenser (Beckman) into 1536-well white plates (Greiner). 4nM final biotin-FKBP12 protein in 50mM HEPES, 50mM NaCl, 5mM MgCl2, 0.02% Brij-35 was dispensed using a Multidrop Combi (Thermo Scientific), followed by addition Tb-streptavidin (Life Technologies) at 2nM final to each well, and incubation at room temp for 1 hour. The plates were read on an Envision plate reader with excitation at 320 nm, and emissions at 520 nm and 492 nm. The 520 nm / 492 nm ratio was used for analysis.

#### ATG16L1 Alphalisa Cleavage Assay

384-well assay-ready plates containing 200nL of 2mM compounds or DMSO were prepared using an I.DOT liquid dispenser (Dispendex). Recombinantly expressed 100nM His-ATG16L1 E44 T300A-Flag (or 50nM His-ATG16L1 WT-Flag) (Table S2) and 20 μM FKBP12 (if present) were diluted in AlphaLISA buffer (20 mM HEPES pH 8, 200 mM NaCl, 1 mM TCEP, 0.05% Tween-20) and 5uL of the resulting solution was added to the compound plate. The plate was then sealed, shaken at 650 rpm for 1 min, spun down, and incubated at 30 °C for 1 hour. 5 uL of recombinantly expressed 50nM caspase-3 (150nM for ATG16L1 WT) was then added to the reaction mixture and incubated at 30 °C for 1 hour (2 hours for ATG16L1 WT). 10uL of a solution containing 20 μΜ Caspase 3 inhibitor (MedChemExpress Z-DEVD-FMK, HY-12466) and 15ng/uL AlphaLISA beads (PerkinElmer AlphaScreen Nickel Chelate Donor Beads AS101M and AlphaLISA anti-Flag Acceptor Beads AL112M) was added to quench the reaction. The solution was incubated at 30°C for 1 hour before the AlphaLISA signal (emission at 615 nm) was measured on the BGM Labtech Pherastar FSX (Broad Alpha, Gain= 3200).

For visualizing by Western blot, 3 technical replicates of protein samples were pooled, loaded and separated by 4-20% bis-tris SDS-PAGE gel (BioRad), transferred onto NC membranes by iBlot 2 (Thermofisher) and blocked in Odyssey blocking buffer (LI-COR; 927-40000) for 1hr at room temperature (RT). After an overnight incubation at 4 °C in Odyssey blocking buffer containing primary antibody [1:5,000 Anti-Flag (CST 14793S)], [1:2,000 Anti FKBP12 (Santa Cruz Biotechnology sc-133067)], blots were washed with Tris-buffered saline containing 0.1% Tween 20 (TBS-T) and incubated for 1hr at RT in secondary antibody solution [1:1 dilution of LI-COR blocking buffer/TBS-T supplemented with 0.02% SDS; 1:10,000 IRDye® 800CW Goat anti-Rabbit IgG Secondary Antibody (Licor 926-32211), 1:10,000 IRDye® 680RD Goat anti-Mouse IgG Secondary Antibody (Licor 926-68070). Blots were imaged using the LI-COR Odyssey infrared imaging system.

#### Caspase-3 activity assay

Recombinantly expressed caspase-3 is diluted in reaction buffer (20mM HEPES pH8, 200mM NaCl, 1mM TCEP, and 0.05% Tween-20) to a final concentration of 250 nM and mixed with DMSO or compound and incubated at 25 °C for 45 minutes. 10.5uL of the mixture is added to Proxiplate 384 Plus plates and fluorescence signal at 460 nm is measured on the SpectraMax M5 for 5 mins to establish a baseline. 14.5 μL of 6.2 μM fluorogenic substrate Ac-DEVD-AMC (MedChemExpress) diluted in reaction buffer is added to reaction wells and fluorescence signal measurement is resumed for 60 mins.

#### Generation of GFP-LC3 expressing HeLa cells

HeLa cells were transduced with lentivirus with GFP-LC344. The media was replaced 48hr posttransduction with DMEM selection media containing puromycin (3μg/ml) for 4 days. The cells were then recovered in the media without puromycin for another 3 days before use.

#### siRNA-mediated knockdown of ATG16L1

siRNA mediated knockdown was performed based on Ambion’s Silencer select RNAi transfection protocol (see Key Resource Table for sequence information). GFP-LC3 expressing HeLa cells were lifted and seeded in 96 well plates at 3000 cells per well prior to transfection. 1.5uL Lipofectamine RNAiMAX reagent (Thermofisher: 13778075) was diluted in 25uL OptiMEM (Thermofisher: 31985070) and combined with 5 pmol of siRNA in 25uL OptiMEM media. The resulting solution was incubated at room temperature for 10 mins, and 10uL of this solution was added to each well containing 90uL media. The media was changed after 8 hours, and the cells were subjected to compound treatment 72 hours post transfection.

#### Bone marrow-derived macrophage (BMDM) isolation

Femurs and tibias were harvested from ATG16L1 WT or T300A mice or from GFP-LC3 reporter mice59 harboring the ATG16L1 T300A mutation and rinsed with ethanol then DMEM supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum, 100U/ml penicillin, 100 mg/ml streptomycin. The ends of the bones are cut off with scissors, and a syringe is inserted into the bone to flush the bone marrow with ~2.5mL DMEM. The combined bone marrow from each bone was pooled and filtered, spun down, resuspended and cultured in DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS, Glutamax, non-essential amino acid, sodium bicarbonate and 20 ng/mL M-CSF (herein referred to as BMDM media) in petri-dishes. On day 7, adherent BMDMs were dissociated from the plate and re-plated for experiments.

#### BMDM ATG16L1 knockouts

1.5 μL of 100 μM pooled ATG16L1 sgRNA or non-targeting control (CRISPRevolution EZ RNA, Synthego) was mixed with 1 μL of 10 mg/mL Alt-R™ S.p. HiFi Cas9 Nuclease V3 (IDT, 1081061) and incubated for 20 minutes, before the addition of 8 μL supplemented P3 nucleofector solution (Lonza). 2 million cells isolated from bone marrow were resuspended in 10 μL of supplemented P3 nucleofector solution (Lonza). The cell suspension and Cas9 ribonucleoprotein solution was mixed and subjected to electroporation using a Lonza 4D-nucleofector X unit (method = CM137). 120 μL BMDM media with 30% FBS was added to the cell suspension after electroporation and incubated for 20 min, before transferring the suspension into a 6 well plate. On day 7, adherent BMDMs were dissociated from the plate and re-plated for experiments.

To visualize knockout efficiency by Western blot, protein samples were loaded and separated by 4-20% bis-tris SDS-PAGE gel (BioRad), transferred onto NC membranes by iBlot 2 (Thermofisher) and blocked in Odyssey blocking buffer (LI-COR; 927-40000) for 1hr at room temperature (RT). After an overnight incubation at 4 °C in Odyssey blocking buffer containing primary antibody [1:1,000 Anti-ATG16L1 (MBL PM040)], [1:10,000 Anti-vinculin (CST 13901S (Rb))], blots were washed with Tris-buffered saline containing 0.1% Tween 20 (TBS-T) and incubated for 1hr at RT in secondary antibody solution [1:1 dilution of LI-COR blocking buffer/TBS-T supplemented with 0.02% SDS; 1:10,000 IRDye® 800CW Goat anti-Rabbit IgG Secondary Antibody (Licor 926-32211). Blots were imaged using the LI-COR Odyssey infrared imaging system.

#### GFP-LC3 puncta assay

HeLa cells or BMDMs expressing GFP-LC3 were seeded at 10,000 or 15,000 cells/well in 96-well plates respectively. On the following day, the media was replaced with 50uL of DMEM containing 5μM rapamycin (MedChemExpress, HY-10219) or 2μM Torin1 (MedChemExpress, HY-13003) plus DEL hits (20μM for HeLa cells, 40μM for BMDMs) and incubated at 37 °C for 4 hours. After treatment, the media was aspirated and the cells were washed with PBS. The cells are then fixed with 4% PFA, washed with PBS, and stained with Hoechst (ThermoFisher, H3570). After staining, the cells were washed with PBS twice before being kept in PBS for imaging. Cells were imaged at 20x for HeLas and 63x for BMDMs using an automated, high-throughput confocal microscope (Perkin Elmer; Opera Phenix). LC3 (488 nm) and DNA (405 nm) images were captured from 15 fields per well for HeLas and 47 fields per well for BMDMs and the area of puncta per cell were quantified using high-content imaging and analysis software (Perkin Elmer; Harmony).

#### Endogenous LC3 immunofluorescence

HeLa cells with WT or T300A ATG16L1 were seeded at 10,000 cells/well in 96-well plates. On the following day, the media was replaced with 50 μL of DMEM containing different treatment compounds and incubated at 37 °C for 4 hours. After treatment, the media was aspirated and the cells were washed with PBS. The cells are fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde and permeabilized with 0.2% saponin for 10 mins at room temperature, followed by washing with PBS containing 0.05% saponin. The cells are blocked with PBS with 5% goat serum and 0.05% saponin for 1 hr, followed by incubation with 1:1000 LC3B primary antibody (MBL international) in PBS with 5% goat serum and 0.05% saponin overnight at 4 °C. On the following day, the cells were washed with PBS with 0.05% saponin 5 times before incubation with secondary Goat Anti-rabbit Alexa Fluor 488 antibody (Invitrogen: A-11034) and Hoechst (ThermoFisher) stain in PBS with 5% goat serum and 0.05% saponin for 40 mins. After 5 additional washes with PBS containing 0.05% saponin, the cells were kept in PBS containing 0.05% saponin for imaging. Cells were imaged at 63x using an automated, high-throughput confocal microscope (Perkin Elmer; Opera Phenix). LC3 (488 nm) and DNA (405 nm) images were captured from 47 fields per well and the area of puncta per cell were quantified using high-content imaging and analysis software (Perkin Elmer; Harmony).

#### LC3-Flux assay

HeLa cells or BMDMs were plated at 120,000 cells per well or 200,000 cells per well in a 24-well plate. The next day the media was replaced with DMEM with or without compound, 5μM rapamycin, and 100nM BafA1 (Millipore Sigma, B1793). For BMDM starvation models, the media was replaced with HBSS with or without compound, and 100nM BafA1. HeLa cells were treated for 4 hours and BMDMs were treated for 3 hours at 37 °C. After which the media was aspirated and 50uL lysis buffer (10mM HEPES, 2mM MgCl2, 1% SDS, 1000x lysonase) containing protease inhibitor cocktail (Roche; 11-873-580-001). The protein samples were loaded and separated by 4-20% bis-tris SDS-PAGE gel (BioRad), transferred onto PVDF membranes by iBlot 2 (Thermofisher) and blocked in Odyssey blocking buffer (LI-COR; 927-40000) for 1hr at room temperature (RT). After an overnight incubation at 4 °C in Odyssey blocking buffer containing primary antibodies [(1:1,000 Anti-LC3B (CST 3868) for HeLa, 1:500 Anti-LC3B (Sigma L7543) for BMDM and 1:10,000 Anti-vinculin (CST 13901S (Rb))], blots were washed with Tris-buffered saline containing 0.1% Tween 20 (TBS-T) and incubated for 1hr at RT in secondary antibody solution [1:1 dilution of LI-COR blocking buffer/TBS-T supplemented with 0.02% SDS; 1:10,000 IRDye® 800CW Goat anti-Rabbit IgG Secondary Antibody (Licor 926-32211). Blots were imaged and quantitated using the LI-COR Odyssey infrared imaging system.

#### S.Typhimurium CFU assay

HeLa cells were plated at 10,000 cells per well in 80μL in 96-well plates (Corning; 3370). A single bacterial colony of S.Typhimurium (SL1344)60 was used to inoculate 5mL LB media and incubated in a shaking incubator at 37 °C O/N. The following day, S.Typhimurium culture was subcultured 1:25 in LB and grown to OD600=1.0. The media was removed from the assay plate and replaced with antibiotic-free media containing S.Typhimurium at an MOI of 100. After 30 min infection at 37 °C in 5% CO2, cells were washed 3 times with DMEM containing 50 μg/mL gentamicin to remove extracellular bacteria. Molecules were added at the appropriate concentration in DMEM containing 20 μg/mL gentamicin and incubated with infected HeLa cells for 6 hrs at 37 °C in 5% CO2. Cells were lysed with 1% Triton-X buffer for 10 min at RT and lysate was used to prepare 10-fold serial dilutions for plating onto LB agar plates. Plates were incubated O/N at 30°C and colonies were counted the following day to determine CFU/mL.

#### S.Typhimurium colocalization assay

GFP-LC3 HeLa cells were plated at 10,000 cells per well in 80μL in 96-well plates (Corning; 3370). A single bacterial colony of S.Typhimurium (SL1344) was used to inoculate 5mL LB media and incubated in a shaking incubator at 37 °C O/N. On the following day, the media was replaced with 40 μL of DMEM containing A3B at 0 or 20 μM and incubated at 37 °C for 3 hours. A S.Typhimurium culture was subcultured 1:25 in LB and grown to OD600=1.0. The culture was diluted 1:10 in DMEM and 10 μL was added to the plate. After 20 min infection at 37 °C in 5% CO2, the media was replaced with DMEM containing 50 μg/mL gentamicin and compound and incubated for 1 hour. The media was aspirated, and the cells were washed with PBS, followed by fixing and permeabilization with ice cold methanol for 8 mins and staining with Hoechst (ThermoFisher). After staining, the cells were washed with PBS twice before being kept in PBS for imaging. Cells were imaged at 63x using an automated, high-throughput confocal microscope (Perkin Elmer; Opera Phenix). LC3 (488 nm) and DNA (405 nm) images were captured from 47 fields per well.

#### Bioluminescent S.Typhimurium replication assay

HeLa, ATG16L1 KO, and ATG16L1 KO reconstituted with WT ATG16L1 cells were plated at 10,000 cells per well in 100μL in 96-well plates (Corning; 3370). A single bacterial colony of S.Typhimurium Xen26 (SL1344) generated previously61 was used to inoculate 5mL LB media with 50 μg/mL Kanamycin and incubated in a shaking incubator at 37 °C O/N. The following day, S.Typhimurium culture was subcultured 1:30 in LB and grown for 3 hours. The media was removed from the assay plate and replaced with antibiotic-free media containing S.Typhimurium at an MOI of 100. After 30 min infection at 37 °C in 5% CO2, cells were washed 2 times with DMEM containing 50 μg/mL gentamicin, and incubated in DMEM containing 50 μg/mL gentamicin for 1 hour at 37°C in 5% CO2 to remove extracellular bacteria. Molecules were added at the appropriate concentration in DMEM containing 20 μg/mL gentamicin and incubated with infected HeLa cells at 37 °C in 5% CO2. Bioluminescence was monitored every hour from the addition of DMSO or A3B using a PHERAstar plate reader with the LUMI module. Fold change was calculated by dividing the bioluminescence of each well at each time point by the bioluminescence of the first reading of the corresponding well at the beginning of compound treatment 1.5h post infection.

#### S. Typhimurium growth curve

A single bacterial colony of S.Typhimurium (SL1344) was used to inoculate 5mL LB media and incubated in a shaking incubator at 37°C O/N. The following day, S.Typhimurium culture was subcultured 1:25 in LB and grown to OD600≅1.0. Salmonella was diluted 1:33 in antibiotic-free DMEM. Molecules were added to a final concentration of 20 μM before adding 100μL of each culture into a 96-well plate and incubated at 37 °C. The growth of S.Typhimurium was monitored by measuring OD600 at fixed time intervals up to 6 hours.

#### IL-1β secretion assay

BMDMs were plated at 10,000 cells per well in 100μL in 96-well plates. After 2 days, the media was replaced with media containing DMSO or compound with 500 ng/mL LPS (Invivogen; tlrl-pb5lps). After priming for 4 hours, ATP (VWR; 0220) was added to a final concentration of 2mM. After 30mins, the supernatant was harvested and the IL-1β was quantified by ELISA (Biotechne R&D; MLB00C).

#### Expression and Protein Purification of ATG16L1 WT and T300A

Table S2 depicts the protein sequence of ATG16L1 constructs. Plasmids consisting of ATG16L1 inserts in pFastBac1 vectors were assembled by Gibson assembly and verified by sanger sequencing (see Key Resource Table for oligonucleotide primers). Plasmids were transformed into DH10Bac competent cells, incubated for 4 hours, plated on Blue-gal agar plates from Teknova (VWR: L1919) and incubated at 37 °C for 48 hours. White colonies were picked, re-streaked on fresh Blue-gal agar plates, and incubated at 37 °C for an additional 48 hours to confirm plasmid selection. A fresh white colony was inoculated into 5 mL of LB with 50 ug/mL kanamycin and grew overnight at 37 °C in a 225-rpm shaking incubator. The culture was centrifuged at 10,000 g for 5 min to collect the pellet. Pellet was processed using a portion of the Qiagen Miniprep Kit to obtain purified Bacmid DNA.

40 mL of SF9 suspension cells was transfected with ATG16L1 bacmid using Cellfectin (ThermoFisher: 10362100) and grew at 27 °C & 140 rpm in an Infors Minitron shaking incubator. After 120-144 hours, the cell viability dropped below 80%, and the P0 virus in suspension was collected using Steriflip filters (MilliporeSigma). Virus was stored at 4 °C in the dark. To generate a higher-titer P1 virus, a new batch of SF9 cells was infected with 100:1 ratio of P0 virus. After 72-96 hours and a drop in cell viability below 60%, the P1 virus in suspension was collected using Steriflip filters. Virus propagation was repeated to generate P2 virus using 100:1 ratio of P1 virus. For multi-liter scale expression of ATG16L1, 100:1 ratio of P2 virus was utilized and infected SF9 cells were grown for 72 hours. After 72 hours, Sf9 cultures were centrifuged at 500g for 10 min to collect the pellet.

Pellets were lysed in Nickel Buffer (50 mM Tris, 250 mM NaCl, 5 mM BME, 5% Glycerol, 20 mM Imidazole, pH 7.5) supplemented with 1X lysonase and 1X EDTA-Free complete Protease Inhibitor Tablets (MilliporeSigma) via Avestin Microfluidizer. After a high-speed spin at 40,000 x g for 30 minutes, the supernatant was incubated with Ni-NTA resin. Resin was washed 3X with Nickel Buffer and transferred to a gravity column. Protein bound to Ni-NTA was eluted with 3 column volumes of Elution Buffer (50 mM Tris, 250 mM NaCl, 5 mM BME, 5% glycerol, 300 mM imidazole, pH 7.5) into 6 fractions of 0.5 CV each. The most concentrated fractions were pooled and purified over a Superdex 200 gel filtration column (Cytiva) that was pre-equilibrated with SEC Buffer (20 mM HEPES, 200 mM NaCl, 5 mM EDTA, 1mM TCEP, 1X complete Protease Inhibitor Tablet). Eluted SEC fractions were quantified by NanoDrop (ThermoFisher), aliquoted, flash frozen by liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C for subsequent experiments.

#### Expression and Protein Purification of Caspase-3

Caspase-3-TEV-6H was generated by GenScript from pET23b-Casp3-His (Addgene: 11821) by inserting a TEV sequence. Caspase-3-TEV-6H was expressed in SHuffle® T7 Competent E. coli cells. Transformed cells were plated on ampicillin-containing LB plates. Single colonies from the plate were grown in 25mL TB. The following day, 20 mL cells were inoculated into a 1L ampicillin-containing TB culture and incubated at 30°C until OD600 reached 0.6. The culture then was induced with 0.5 mM IPTG and incubated overnight at 20°C in a shaker. The culture was spun down at 5000 rpm for 10 minutes and the supernatant was discarded. Pellets were lysed in Nickel Buffer (20 mM Tris pH 8, 250 mM NaCl, 10% Glycerol, 25 mM Imidazole) supplemented with 1X lysonase and 1X EDTA-Free cOmplete Protease Inhibitor Tablets (MilliporeSigma) via Avestin Microfluidizer. After a high-speed spin at 30,000 x g for 45 minutes at 4°C, the supernatant was incubated with Ni-NTA resin. Resin was washed 3X with Nickel Buffer and transferred to a gravity column. Protein bound to Ni-NTA was eluted with 3 column volumes of Elution Buffer (20 mM Tris pH 8, 250 mM NaCl, 10% Glycerol, 1M imidazole) into 6 fractions of 0.5 CV each. The most concentrated fractions were pooled and purified over a Superdex 200 gel filtration column (Cytiva) that was pre-equilibrated with SEC Buffer (20 mM Tris pH 8, 250 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol). Eluted SEC fractions were pooled and quantified by NanoDrop (ThermoFisher). His-tagged TEV protease was added at a 10:1 Caspase-3: TEV protease to cleave off the His-tag. After confirming that cleavage proceeded via a Coomassie-stained SDS-PAGE gel, the protein solution was incubated with Ni-NTA resin for an hour at 4 °C. The mixture was transferred to a gravity column and the flowthrough containing cleaved tagless Caspase-3 was collected. Buffer exchange was performed to replace the imidazole containing buffer to the SEC buffer, and the final Caspase-3 was quantified by NanoDrop (ThermoFisher), aliquoted, flash frozen by liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C for subsequent experiments.

#### General methods

All air or moisture sensitive reactions were performed under positive pressure of nitrogen with oven dried glassware under N2 atmosphere. Chemical reagents and anhydrous solvents were obtained from commercial sources and used as-is. Reaction progress was monitored by analytical thin-layer chromatography (TLC) using E. Merck silica gel 60 F254 pre-coated plates (250 μm), or by tandem liquid chromatography/mass spectrometry (LCMS) using a Waters 2795 separations module and 3100 mass detector. Low-resolution mass spectrometry (LRMS) data were also collected using this instrument. Compound spots were visualized by UV light (254 nm) and potassium permanganate staining. RP-Preparative HPLC was performed using a Teledyne ISCO ACCQPrep HP150 instrument equipped with an XBridge C18 column (19 x 250 mm, 5 μm with a gradient of 10-100% MeCN-H2O (both solvents contain 0.1% Formic acid). Chemical shifts are reported in parts per million (ppm) relative to the appropriate solvent—CDCl3: 7.26 (1H), 77.16 (13C) ppm; (CD3)2SO: 2.50 (1H), 39.52 (13C) ppm; CD3OD: 3.31 (1H), 49.00 (13C) ppm. #### General procedure for connector synthesis

#### Method A write up

To a solution of mono-Boc protected amine (1 eq) and Et3N (1.2 eq) in DCM (0.1M) was added NsCl (1.05 eq). Reaction was monitored by LC-MS, and is usually done within 1 hour. The resulting solution was washed with water and extracted with DCM (2x). The combined organic layers were dried over anhydrous Mg2SO4, filtered and concentrated. The crude material was used in the next step directly without further purification. The crude material was dissolved in DCM (0.1M) and TFA was added to result in a 4:1 DCM:TFA solution. The reaction was stirred at room temperature for 2 hours, followed by removal of solvents in vacuo and azeotropic removal with toluene 2x. The final product was purified with silica gel chromatography (1% Et3N in DCM:MeOH).

#### Method B

To a solution of mono-Boc protected amine (1 eq) and Et3N (2.4 eq) in DCM (0.1M) was added FmocCl (1.1 eq). After stirring for 5 hours, the resulting solution was washed with water and extracted with DCM (2x). The combined organic layers were dried over anhydrous Mg2SO4, filtered and concentrated, and purified with silica gel chromatography (1% Et3N in DCM:MeOH). The Fmoc-protected amine was dissolved in DCM (0.1M) and TFA was added to result in a 4:1 DCM TFA solution. The reaction was stirred at room temperature for 2 hours, followed by removal of solvents in vacuo and azeotropic removal with toluene 2x. To a solution of crude mono-Fmoc protected amine (1 eq) and Et3N (6-10 eq) in DCM (0.1M) was added NsCl (1.05 eq). Reaction was monitored by LC-MS, and is usually done within 1 hour. Solvents are removed in vacuo, and the residue was redissolved in DMF (0.1M) with 20% piperidine. After stirring for 1-4 hours, the solvents were removed and the mono-Ns protected amine was purified by silica gel chromatography (1% Et3N in DCM:MeOH).

#### Method C

To a solution of amine (5 eq) and Et3N (1.5 eq) in DCM (0.02M) at 0 °C was added NsCl (1.0 eq) in DCM dropwise. After 1 hour, the resulting mixture was filtered over celite, concentrated in vacuo, and purified with silica gel chromatography (1% Et3N in DCM:MeOH) to afford the product.

### Ion-pair chromatographic analysis of DNA conjugates by UPLC–MS

Samples were resolved on a Waters ACQUITY system equipped with a C18 column (ACQUITY Oligonucleotide BEH C18 1.7 μm, 2.1 × 50 mm, part #186003949) kept at 50 °C. UV signal was recorded with an ACQUITY TUV detector (260 nm, sampling rate 20 points/s). Mass spectra of eluting species were recorded with a Waters SQ Detector 2 connected to a ZSprayTM source (negative ion mode, scan time 0.2 s, scanning range 500–3000 Da, MaxEnt1 deconvolution, processing 2-20 kDa). For the standard method (5–50% B), the following conditions were used: flow–0.5 mL/min, runtime 6.0 min, injection volume 10 μL, temp 50 °C. The column used was the ACQUITY Oligonucleotide BEH C18 1.7 μM, 2.1 × 50 mm. Solvent A was 250 mM hexafluoroisopropanol and 8 mM NEt3 in water. Solvent B was methanol. Run conditions were as follows: 0.0–4.0 min 95% solvent A, 5% solvent B; 4.0–4.5 min 50% solvent A, 50% solvent B; 4.5–5.1 min 5% solvent A, 95% solvent B; 5.1–6.0 min 95% solvent A, 5% solvent B. Full UPLC-MS traces of DNA conjugates can be found in Data S1.

### Ethanol precipitation

To a reaction of a given volume (100% v/v), aq. NaCl (5 M, 10% v/v) and EtOH (300-500% v/v) were added. The reaction vessel was briefly vortexed and incubated on dry ice for 30 to 60 min. After centrifugation (10–20 min at 3750 x g), the supernatant was removed by decanting into another vessel. To wash the pellet, 80% aq. EtOH (300% v/v) was added. The mixture was vortexed for approximately 2 min and chilled again on dry ice for approximately 10 min. After centrifugation (10–20 min at 3750 x g), the supernatant was removed by decanting into another vessel. The washing procedure was repeated with 100% EtOH (300% v/v) and the obtained pellet was dried under vacuum.

### Preparative HPLC of oligonucleotide conjugates

Purifications were performed on an Agilent Infinity system equipped with an Infinity 1260 Bio Quat Pump (pump system, G5611A), an Infinity 1260 HiP Bio ALS (autosampler, G1330B), an Infinity 1290 TCC (thermostatted column compartment, G5667A), an Infinity 1260 DAD (diode array detector, G4212B), and an Infinity 1260 Bio FC-AS (fraction collector, G5664A) under Agilent OpenLab CDS (C.01.07 SR1) software control. The column (Waters XBridge BEH C18 OBD, 130 Å, 5 μm, 10 × 150 mm) was kept at 50 °C. Material was injected as aqueous solutions (up to 100 μL per injection) and eluted with gradients of solvent A (50 mM triethylammonium acetate in water) and solvent B (MeOH). Fraction collection was triggered by UV (260 nm). The following 5–50% method was used: flow 5.0 mL/min, runtime 20 min, column used was Waters XBridge BEH C18 OBD, 130 Å, 5 μm, 10 × 150 mm. The run conditions were as follows: 0.0–15.0 min 90% solvent A, 10% solvent B; 15.0–16.0 min 30% solvent A, 70% solvent B; 16.0–18.1 min 5% solvent A, 95% solvent B; 18.1–20.0 min 95% solvent A, 5% solvent B.

Following separation, desired species-containing fractions were pooled and concentrated by ultrafiltration (Millipore Amicon Ultra-15/4 centrifugal filters; Ultracel 10 K/3 K) according to manufacturer guidelines. Three cycles of sample concentration/buffer dilution with nuclease-free water were employed.

### Synthesis of FKBP CIP-DEL

#### Synthesis of N3-HP-DNA

To a 1 Dram vial with septum was added EDC (0.096 g, 0.5 mmol, 1.0 eq), DMF (1.0mL), and 2-azidoacetic acid (0.045 mL, 0.600 mmol, 1.2 eq) (via pipette); the mixture was stirred for 3 minutes (turning into yellow solution), before a solution of N-hydroxysuccinimide (0.063 g, 0.550 mmol, 1.1 eq) in DMF (0.25 mL) was added via syringe.

After stirring for 2 hrs, the resulting solution of 2,5-dioxopyrrolidin-1-yl 2-azidoacetate (assume 400mM in DMF) was used directly in the next step.

A solution of 2,5-dioxopyrrolidin-1-yl 2-azidoacetate (400 mM in DMF, 40 eq) was added to 1mM DNA-AOP headpiece (4.68 μmol, 1 eq) in aqueous sodium borate buffer (150 mM, pH 9.4). After an hour at rt, the reaction was subjected to EtOH precipitation and used in the next step without further purification. Yield >99%. Expected mass 5265, observed 5267.

#### General method D for preparation of DNA conjugates containing nosylated-connectors

To a solution of DEL Precursor (20 eq), Ns-protected amine (30 eq) and DIPEA (60 eq) in DMF (0.2M) was added HATU (24 eq). The resulting yellow solution was stirred at room temperature for 6 hours. The solution was transferred to an 1.5mL eppendorf tube, and was added was added N3-HP-DNA (1 eq, 1mM in PBS pH 8), sodium ascorbate (10 eq, 500mM in H2O), TBTA (10 eq, 200 mM in 4:1 tBuOH:DMSO) and CuSO4 (10 eq, 500mM in H2O). The reaction mixture was shaken overnight. After the addition of sodium diethyldithiocarbamate (125 eq, 100 mmolar), the brown mixture was vortexed vigorously then centrifuged at 13000 g for 5 mins. The supernatant was subjected to ethanol precipitation. The DNA-conjugates 5 were purified by preparative HPLC to afford products with yields of 8 - 30%.
